Respiratory Illness Outbreak Disrupts Panama Electric Utilities Sector

A sudden outbreak of an acute respiratory illness has caused significant disruptions across Panama’s electric utilities sector, with dozens of workers reportedly hospitalized and several power generation facilities operating at reduced capacity. The outbreak, which was first detected late last week at the Chorrera Hydroelectric Plant, has since been confirmed at three additional sites, according to reports from the National Utilities Workers’ Union (SUNPE).

As of Wednesday, the Ministry of Health has counted 57 confirmed cases among industry employees, mainly affecting shift operators, maintenance crews, and administrative staff. While health officials have not yet identified the exact pathogen responsible, preliminary assessments indicate the illness spreads rapidly in enclosed work environments.

The impact on daily operations has been immediate. “We are currently running at 60% staffing levels at our core facilities,” said Alejandro Mendoza, spokesperson for the state-owned LuzPanama. “Our teams are working double shifts to maintain a stable power supply, but the situation is challenging.” Mendoza noted that, although no major blackouts have been reported, routine maintenance and network upgrades have been postponed indefinitely.

Local energy analyst Rosa Salazar expressed concern over the sustainability of current measures. “The industry is highly dependent on specialized technical staff,” Salazar commented. “With so many out sick, even minor faults risk escalating into more serious service interruptions.”

In an official statement, the Ministry of Labor urged electric utility employers to implement stricter health and safety protocols, including mandatory mask use, staggered shifts, and enhanced ventilation at all operational sites. Some companies, such as Energia Istmeña, have begun providing temporary accommodation for essential staff to limit outside contact.

Union leaders, meanwhile, are calling for urgent government support. “Our members are on the front lines, keeping the lights on for the country,” said SUNPE president Jorge Villarreal. “We need personal protective equipment, paid sick leave guarantees, and clear communication from management.”

The Ministry of Health has dispatched epidemiological teams to affected facilities and is coordinating with companies to conduct mass testing. As the investigation continues, officials are urging all electric utilities workers experiencing symptoms to self-isolate and seek medical attention.

Authorities have not provided an estimate for when the outbreak may be contained, but industry insiders warn that ongoing workforce shortages could continue to strain Panama’s electricity supply in the coming weeks.
